case_info.scenario: A 16-year-old male with a history of mild seasonal allergies presented with right-sided congestion, thick discolored nasal drainage, facial pain/pressure, anosmia, and intermittent epistaxis for approximately 1 year. Nasal endoscopy revealed moderate global deviation of the septum to the left. On the right, thick mucus and crusting anterior to the middle turbinate was seen, completely occluding the nasal cavity. Physical examination was otherwise normal. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a heterogeneous, expansile mass measuring 6 (anteroposterior) × 3.1 (transverse) × 5 (craniocaudal) cm within the right nasal cavity extending to the nasopharynx, with obliteration of the nasopharyngeal airway and anteroinferior displacement of the soft palate (Figure, B). The adjacent sinuses had drainage obstruction. Biopsy results showed fragments of necrotic and fibrinous debris with acute inflammatory exudate and bacterial colonies. Findings during surgery included a fibrous expansile mass filling the right nasal cavity and bowing the septum to the left. It crossed the midline to fill the nasopharynx and extended inferiorly toward the oropharynx. The mass was noted to originate at the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus. Pathologic evaluation showed fragments of polypoidal mucosa with edematous stroma, numerous ectatic vascular channels, and a sprinkling of inflammatory cells (Figure, A). The surface epithelium was largely ulcerated, covered with fibrinous and inflammatory debris and bacterial colonies. Immunostaining showed CD31 and CD34 positivity. Stromal cells did not have β-catenin present. Elastic stain results showed scant elastic fibers in the vascular proliferation.
case_info.caption: A, Low-powered hematoxylin-eosin stain of polypoidal mucosa with edematous stroma and numerous ectatic vascular channels (original magnification ×200). B, Coronal postcontrast T1 fat-saturated image acquired in a 3-T magnet.
case_info.explanation: Of the 5 histological subtypes of sinonasal polyps (edematous, glandular, fibrous, cystic, and angiomatous or angiectatic), angiomatous nasal polyps (ANPs) make up about 4% to 5% of these sinonasal lesions.1Sinonasal polyps may present with nasal obstruction, facial pain or pressure, snoring, anosmia, epistaxis, and nasal drainage.2Some reports of ANPs describe a foul odor associated with the lesions, raising concern for bacterial, fungal, or malignant processes.3These presenting symptoms, however, are nonspecific, and additional workup must be completed to assess for other causes, such as inverted papilloma (IP), sinonasal tract angiofibroma (STA), and lobular capillary hemangioma (LCH). On computed tomography, ANPs typically present as a heterogenous density with minimal enhancement at the lesion’s edges and accompanying bony changes.4When visualized on magnetic resonance imaging, ANPs display heterogeneous isointense signal intensity on T1-weighted images and a hypointense peripheral rim on T2-weighted images.5IPs may have similar imaging appearance and display hypointense T1 signal with isointense or hypointense signal on T2-weighted image; contrast enhancement is in a convoluted cerebriform pattern.6Imaging of LCHs often show bone destruction and evidence of phleboliths.7STAs typically demonstrate heterogenous signal intensity on T1-weighted images and may be either high intensity or isointensity predominant on T2-weighted images.8Internal flow voids and intense enhancement are also seen in the majority of STAs, as well as LCHs.7In STAs, involvement of the sphenopalatine foramen/pterygopalatine fossa is often present,8which is not seen in ANPs. Location of origin is another factor that may differentiate these tumors. ANPs typically originate from the maxillary sinus and may spread to the choana.4LCHs most commonly originate from the anterior nasal septum, while STAs originate from the sphenopalatine foramen region along the posterior nasal cavity.7Alternatively, IPs usually arise from the lateral nasal wall or the paranasal sinuses. Imaging findings for this patient reflect ANP, with a large heterogeneous expansile mass extending from the right nasal cavity to the nasopharynx and into the posterior aspect of the maxillary sinus, with mass effect and mild resorption of the surrounding bones. When examined via light microscopy, ANPs often have an ulcerated roof and areas lined by respiratory epithelium, which may show squamous metaplasia.2ANPs also show scattered atypical pleomorphic spindle cells in the stroma, a paucity of inflammatory infiltrate, and abundant amorphous, Congo red–negative material.1ANPs are characterized by a high degree of vascular proliferation and ectasia; as such, these blood vessels may be subject to compression leading to infarction.3Given the highly vascularized and potentially necrotic nature of ANPs, it is understandable that these polyps may present with diagnostic difficulty due to potential confusion with other vascular tumors. Fully developed LCHs typically display lobules of back-to-back capillaries, with endothelial cells divided by fibrous or myxoid septa.9STAs, on the other hand, demonstrate a dense stromal component with numerous fibroblasts and have varying levels of vessel density. Immunohistochemical stains are also helpful in differentiating STAs from other tumors and will be positive for β-catenin, androgen receptor, estrogen receptor β, and prostate-specific antigen.7IPs are characterized histologically by an inverted appearance due to thickened epithelium enclosed by basement membrane, along with transmigrating intraepithelial neutrophilic inflammation.6The pathology and immunohistochemistry findings, as outlined in this case, align with ANP. The standard treatment for ANPs is resection via endoscopic approach. This treatment allows for symptom relief and a definitive pathologic characterization. Removal of the site of origin of these polyps is crucial for preventing recurrence. The present patient underwent successful endoscopic resection and followed up regularly outpatient after surgery. The patient’s presenting symptoms have resolved, and there was no evidence of recurrence at 6 months.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Of the 5 histological subtypes of sinonasal polyps (edematous, glandular, fibrous, cystic, and angiomatous or angiectatic), angiomatous nasal polyps (ANPs) make up about 4% to 5% of these sinonasal lesions.1Sinonasal polyps may present with nasal obstruction, facial pain or pressure, snoring, anosmia, epistaxis, and nasal drainage.2Some reports of ANPs describe a foul odor associated with the lesions, raising concern for bacterial, fungal, or malignant processes.3These presenting symptoms, however, are nonspecific, and additional workup must be completed to assess for other causes, such as inverted papilloma (IP), sinonasal tract angiofibroma (STA), and lobular capillary hemangioma (LCH). On computed tomography, ANPs typically present as a heterogenous density with minimal enhancement at the lesion’s edges and accompanying bony changes.4When visualized on magnetic resonance imaging, ANPs display heterogeneous isointense signal intensity on T1-weighted images and a hypointense peripheral rim on T2-weighted images.5IPs may have similar imaging appearance and display hypointense T1 signal with isointense or hypointense signal on T2-weighted image; contrast enhancement is in a convoluted cerebriform pattern.6Imaging of LCHs often show bone destruction and evidence of phleboliths.7STAs typically demonstrate heterogenous signal intensity on T1-weighted images and may be either high intensity or isointensity predominant on T2-weighted images.8Internal flow voids and intense enhancement are also seen in the majority of STAs, as well as LCHs.7In STAs, involvement of the sphenopalatine foramen/pterygopalatine fossa is often present,8which is not seen in ANPs. Location of origin is another factor that may differentiate these tumors. ANPs typically originate from the maxillary sinus and may spread to the choana.4LCHs most commonly originate from the anterior nasal septum, while STAs originate from the sphenopalatine foramen region along the posterior nasal cavity.7Alternatively, IPs usually arise from the lateral nasal wall or the paranasal sinuses. Imaging findings for this patient reflect ANP, with a large heterogeneous expansile mass extending from the right nasal cavity to the nasopharynx and into the posterior aspect of the maxillary sinus, with mass effect and mild resorption of the surrounding bones. When examined via light microscopy, ANPs often have an ulcerated roof and areas lined by respiratory epithelium, which may show squamous metaplasia.2ANPs also show scattered atypical pleomorphic spindle cells in the stroma, a paucity of inflammatory infiltrate, and abundant amorphous, Congo red–negative material.1ANPs are characterized by a high degree of vascular proliferation and ectasia; as such, these blood vessels may be subject to compression leading to infarction.3Given the highly vascularized and potentially necrotic nature of ANPs, it is understandable that these polyps may present with diagnostic difficulty due to potential confusion with other vascular tumors. Fully developed LCHs typically display lobules of back-to-back capillaries, with endothelial cells divided by fibrous or myxoid septa.9STAs, on the other hand, demonstrate a dense stromal component with numerous fibroblasts and have varying levels of vessel density. Immunohistochemical stains are also helpful in differentiating STAs from other tumors and will be positive for β-catenin, androgen receptor, estrogen receptor β, and prostate-specific antigen.7IPs are characterized histologically by an inverted appearance due to thickened epithelium enclosed by basement membrane, along with transmigrating intraepithelial neutrophilic inflammation.6The pathology and immunohistochemistry findings, as outlined in this case, align with ANP. The standard treatment for ANPs is resection via endoscopic approach. This treatment allows for symptom relief and a definitive pathologic characterization. Removal of the site of origin of these polyps is crucial for preventing recurrence. The present patient underwent successful endoscopic resection and followed up regularly outpatient after surgery. The patient’s presenting symptoms have resolved, and there was no evidence of recurrence at 6 months.

   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication

case_info.explanation: Of the 5 histological subtypes of sinonasal polyps (edematous, glandular, fibrous, cystic, and angiomatous or angiectatic), angiomatous nasal polyps (ANPs) make up about 4% to 5% of these sinonasal lesions.1Sinonasal polyps may present with nasal obstruction, facial pain or pressure, snoring, anosmia, epistaxis, and nasal drainage.2Some reports of ANPs describe a foul odor associated with the lesions, raising concern for bacterial, fungal, or malignant processes.3These presenting symptoms, however, are nonspecific, and additional workup must be completed to assess for other causes, such as inverted papilloma (IP), sinonasal tract angiofibroma (STA), and lobular capillary hemangioma (LCH). On computed tomography, ANPs typically present as a heterogenous density with minimal enhancement at the lesion’s edges and accompanying bony changes.4When visualized on magnetic resonance imaging, ANPs display heterogeneous isointense signal intensity on T1-weighted images and a hypointense peripheral rim on T2-weighted images.5IPs may have similar imaging appearance and display hypointense T1 signal with isointense or hypointense signal on T2-weighted image; contrast enhancement is in a convoluted cerebriform pattern.6Imaging of LCHs often show bone destruction and evidence of phleboliths.7STAs typically demonstrate heterogenous signal intensity on T1-weighted images and may be either high intensity or isointensity predominant on T2-weighted images.8Internal flow voids and intense enhancement are also seen in the majority of STAs, as well as LCHs.7In STAs, involvement of the sphenopalatine foramen/pterygopalatine fossa is often present,8which is not seen in ANPs. Location of origin is another factor that may differentiate these tumors. ANPs typically originate from the maxillary sinus and may spread to the choana.4LCHs most commonly originate from the anterior nasal septum, while STAs originate from the sphenopalatine foramen region along the posterior nasal cavity.7Alternatively, IPs usually arise from the lateral nasal wall or the paranasal sinuses. Imaging findings for this patient reflect ANP, with a large heterogeneous expansile mass extending from the right nasal cavity to the nasopharynx and into the posterior aspect of the maxillary sinus, with mass effect and mild resorption of the surrounding bones. When examined via light microscopy, ANPs often have an ulcerated roof and areas lined by respiratory epithelium, which may show squamous metaplasia.2ANPs also show scattered atypical pleomorphic spindle cells in the stroma, a paucity of inflammatory infiltrate, and abundant amorphous, Congo red–negative material.1ANPs are characterized by a high degree of vascular proliferation and ectasia; as such, these blood vessels may be subject to compression leading to infarction.3Given the highly vascularized and potentially necrotic nature of ANPs, it is understandable that these polyps may present with diagnostic difficulty due to potential confusion with other vascular tumors. Fully developed LCHs typically display lobules of back-to-back capillaries, with endothelial cells divided by fibrous or myxoid septa.9STAs, on the other hand, demonstrate a dense stromal component with numerous fibroblasts and have varying levels of vessel density. Immunohistochemical stains are also helpful in differentiating STAs from other tumors and will be positive for β-catenin, androgen receptor, estrogen receptor β, and prostate-specific antigen.7IPs are characterized histologically by an inverted appearance due to thickened epithelium enclosed by basement membrane, along with transmigrating intraepithelial neutrophilic inflammation.6The pathology and immunohistochemistry findings, as outlined in this case, align with ANP. The standard treatment for ANPs is resection via endoscopic approach. This treatment allows for symptom relief and a definitive pathologic characterization. Removal of the site of origin of these polyps is crucial for preventing recurrence. The present patient underwent successful endoscopic resection and followed up regularly outpatient after surgery. The patient’s presenting symptoms have resolved, and there was no evidence of recurrence at 6 months.

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting

       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams

       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or

       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,

2. Performance
   Definition:

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.

case_info.explanation: Of the 5 histological subtypes of sinonasal polyps (edematous, glandular, fibrous, cystic, and angiomatous or angiectatic), angiomatous nasal polyps (ANPs) make up about 4% to 5% of these sinonasal lesions.1Sinonasal polyps may present with nasal obstruction, facial pain or pressure, snoring, anosmia, epistaxis, and nasal drainage.2Some reports of ANPs describe a foul odor associated with the lesions, raising concern for bacterial, fungal, or malignant processes.3These presenting symptoms, however, are nonspecific, and additional workup must be completed to assess for other causes, such as inverted papilloma (IP), sinonasal tract angiofibroma (STA), and lobular capillary hemangioma (LCH). On computed tomography, ANPs typically present as a heterogenous density with minimal enhancement at the lesion’s edges and accompanying bony changes.4When visualized on magnetic resonance imaging, ANPs display heterogeneous isointense signal intensity on T1-weighted images and a hypointense peripheral rim on T2-weighted images.5IPs may have similar imaging appearance and display hypointense T1 signal with isointense or hypointense signal on T2-weighted image; contrast enhancement is in a convoluted cerebriform pattern.6Imaging of LCHs often show bone destruction and evidence of phleboliths.7STAs typically demonstrate heterogenous signal intensity on T1-weighted images and may be either high intensity or isointensity predominant on T2-weighted images.8Internal flow voids and intense enhancement are also seen in the majority of STAs, as well as LCHs.7In STAs, involvement of the sphenopalatine foramen/pterygopalatine fossa is often present,8which is not seen in ANPs. Location of origin is another factor that may differentiate these tumors. ANPs typically originate from the maxillary sinus and may spread to the choana.4LCHs most commonly originate from the anterior nasal septum, while STAs originate from the sphenopalatine foramen region along the posterior nasal cavity.7Alternatively, IPs usually arise from the lateral nasal wall or the paranasal sinuses. Imaging findings for this patient reflect ANP, with a large heterogeneous expansile mass extending from the right nasal cavity to the nasopharynx and into the posterior aspect of the maxillary sinus, with mass effect and mild resorption of the surrounding bones. When examined via light microscopy, ANPs often have an ulcerated roof and areas lined by respiratory epithelium, which may show squamous metaplasia.2ANPs also show scattered atypical pleomorphic spindle cells in the stroma, a paucity of inflammatory infiltrate, and abundant amorphous, Congo red–negative material.1ANPs are characterized by a high degree of vascular proliferation and ectasia; as such, these blood vessels may be subject to compression leading to infarction.3Given the highly vascularized and potentially necrotic nature of ANPs, it is understandable that these polyps may present with diagnostic difficulty due to potential confusion with other vascular tumors. Fully developed LCHs typically display lobules of back-to-back capillaries, with endothelial cells divided by fibrous or myxoid septa.9STAs, on the other hand, demonstrate a dense stromal component with numerous fibroblasts and have varying levels of vessel density. Immunohistochemical stains are also helpful in differentiating STAs from other tumors and will be positive for β-catenin, androgen receptor, estrogen receptor β, and prostate-specific antigen.7IPs are characterized histologically by an inverted appearance due to thickened epithelium enclosed by basement membrane, along with transmigrating intraepithelial neutrophilic inflammation.6The pathology and immunohistochemistry findings, as outlined in this case, align with ANP. The standard treatment for ANPs is resection via endoscopic approach. This treatment allows for symptom relief and a definitive pathologic characterization. Removal of the site of origin of these polyps is crucial for preventing recurrence. The present patient underwent successful endoscopic resection and followed up regularly outpatient after surgery. The patient’s presenting symptoms have resolved, and there was no evidence of recurrence at 6 months.

case_info.explanation: Of the 5 histological subtypes of sinonasal polyps (edematous, glandular, fibrous, cystic, and angiomatous or angiectatic), angiomatous nasal polyps (ANPs) make up about 4% to 5% of these sinonasal lesions.1Sinonasal polyps may present with nasal obstruction, facial pain or pressure, snoring, anosmia, epistaxis, and nasal drainage.2Some reports of ANPs describe a foul odor associated with the lesions, raising concern for bacterial, fungal, or malignant processes.3These presenting symptoms, however, are nonspecific, and additional workup must be completed to assess for other causes, such as inverted papilloma (IP), sinonasal tract angiofibroma (STA), and lobular capillary hemangioma (LCH). On computed tomography, ANPs typically present as a heterogenous density with minimal enhancement at the lesion’s edges and accompanying bony changes.4When visualized on magnetic resonance imaging, ANPs display heterogeneous isointense signal intensity on T1-weighted images and a hypointense peripheral rim on T2-weighted images.5IPs may have similar imaging appearance and display hypointense T1 signal with isointense or hypointense signal on T2-weighted image; contrast enhancement is in a convoluted cerebriform pattern.6Imaging of LCHs often show bone destruction and evidence of phleboliths.7STAs typically demonstrate heterogenous signal intensity on T1-weighted images and may be either high intensity or isointensity predominant on T2-weighted images.8Internal flow voids and intense enhancement are also seen in the majority of STAs, as well as LCHs.7In STAs, involvement of the sphenopalatine foramen/pterygopalatine fossa is often present,8which is not seen in ANPs. Location of origin is another factor that may differentiate these tumors. ANPs typically originate from the maxillary sinus and may spread to the choana.4LCHs most commonly originate from the anterior nasal septum, while STAs originate from the sphenopalatine foramen region along the posterior nasal cavity.7Alternatively, IPs usually arise from the lateral nasal wall or the paranasal sinuses. Imaging findings for this patient reflect ANP, with a large heterogeneous expansile mass extending from the right nasal cavity to the nasopharynx and into the posterior aspect of the maxillary sinus, with mass effect and mild resorption of the surrounding bones. When examined via light microscopy, ANPs often have an ulcerated roof and areas lined by respiratory epithelium, which may show squamous metaplasia.2ANPs also show scattered atypical pleomorphic spindle cells in the stroma, a paucity of inflammatory infiltrate, and abundant amorphous, Congo red–negative material.1ANPs are characterized by a high degree of vascular proliferation and ectasia; as such, these blood vessels may be subject to compression leading to infarction.3Given the highly vascularized and potentially necrotic nature of ANPs, it is understandable that these polyps may present with diagnostic difficulty due to potential confusion with other vascular tumors. Fully developed LCHs typically display lobules of back-to-back capillaries, with endothelial cells divided by fibrous or myxoid septa.9STAs, on the other hand, demonstrate a dense stromal component with numerous fibroblasts and have varying levels of vessel density. Immunohistochemical stains are also helpful in differentiating STAs from other tumors and will be positive for β-catenin, androgen receptor, estrogen receptor β, and prostate-specific antigen.7IPs are characterized histologically by an inverted appearance due to thickened epithelium enclosed by basement membrane, along with transmigrating intraepithelial neutrophilic inflammation.6The pathology and immunohistochemistry findings, as outlined in this case, align with ANP. The standard treatment for ANPs is resection via endoscopic approach. This treatment allows for symptom relief and a definitive pathologic characterization. Removal of the site of origin of these polyps is crucial for preventing recurrence. The present patient underwent successful endoscopic resection and followed up regularly outpatient after surgery. The patient’s presenting symptoms have resolved, and there was no evidence of recurrence at 6 months.

case_info.scenario: A 16-year-old male with a history of mild seasonal allergies presented with right-sided congestion, thick discolored nasal drainage, facial pain/pressure, anosmia, and intermittent epistaxis for approximately 1 year. The adjacent sinuses had drainage obstruction. Biopsy results showed fragments of necrotic and fibrinous debris with acute inflammatory exudate and bacterial colonies. Findings during surgery included a fibrous expansile mass filling the right nasal cavity and bowing the septum to the left. case_info.explanation: Of the 5 histological subtypes of sinonasal polyps (edematous, glandular, fibrous, cystic, and angiomatous or angiectatic), angiomatous nasal polyps (ANPs) make up about 4% to 5% of these sinonasal lesions.1Sinonasal polyps may present with nasal obstruction, facial pain or pressure, snoring, anosmia, epistaxis, and nasal drainage.2Some reports of ANPs describe a foul odor associated with the lesions, raising concern for bacterial, fungal, or malignant processes.3These presenting symptoms, however, are nonspecific, and additional workup must be completed to assess for other causes, such as inverted papilloma (IP), sinonasal tract angiofibroma (STA), and lobular capillary hemangioma (LCH). On computed tomography, ANPs typically present as a heterogenous density with minimal enhancement at the lesion’s edges and accompanying bony changes.4When visualized on magnetic resonance imaging, ANPs display heterogeneous isointense signal intensity on T1-weighted images and a hypointense peripheral rim on T2-weighted images.5IPs may have similar imaging appearance and display hypointense T1 signal with isointense or hypointense signal on T2-weighted image; contrast enhancement is in a convoluted cerebriform pattern.6Imaging of LCHs often show bone destruction and evidence of phleboliths.7STAs typically demonstrate heterogenous signal intensity on T1-weighted images and may be either high intensity or isointensity predominant on T2-weighted images.8Internal flow voids and intense enhancement are also seen in the majority of STAs, as well as LCHs.7In STAs, involvement of the sphenopalatine foramen/pterygopalatine fossa is often present,8which is not seen in ANPs. Location of origin is another factor that may differentiate these tumors. ANPs typically originate from the maxillary sinus and may spread to the choana.4LCHs most commonly originate from the anterior nasal septum, while STAs originate from the sphenopalatine foramen region along the posterior nasal cavity.7Alternatively, IPs usually arise from the lateral nasal wall or the paranasal sinuses. Imaging findings for this patient reflect ANP, with a large heterogeneous expansile mass extending from the right nasal cavity to the nasopharynx and into the posterior aspect of the maxillary sinus, with mass effect and mild resorption of the surrounding bones. When examined via light microscopy, ANPs often have an ulcerated roof and areas lined by respiratory epithelium, which may show squamous metaplasia.2ANPs also show scattered atypical pleomorphic spindle cells in the stroma, a paucity of inflammatory infiltrate, and abundant amorphous, Congo red–negative material.1ANPs are characterized by a high degree of vascular proliferation and ectasia; as such, these blood vessels may be subject to compression leading to infarction.3Given the highly vascularized and potentially necrotic nature of ANPs, it is understandable that these polyps may present with diagnostic difficulty due to potential confusion with other vascular tumors. Fully developed LCHs typically display lobules of back-to-back capillaries, with endothelial cells divided by fibrous or myxoid septa.9STAs, on the other hand, demonstrate a dense stromal component with numerous fibroblasts and have varying levels of vessel density. Immunohistochemical stains are also helpful in differentiating STAs from other tumors and will be positive for β-catenin, androgen receptor, estrogen receptor β, and prostate-specific antigen.7IPs are characterized histologically by an inverted appearance due to thickened epithelium enclosed by basement membrane, along with transmigrating intraepithelial neutrophilic inflammation.6The pathology and immunohistochemistry findings, as outlined in this case, align with ANP. The standard treatment for ANPs is resection via endoscopic approach. This treatment allows for symptom relief and a definitive pathologic characterization. Removal of the site of origin of these polyps is crucial for preventing recurrence. The present patient underwent successful endoscopic resection and followed up regularly outpatient after surgery. The patient’s presenting symptoms have resolved, and there was no evidence of recurrence at 6 months.

Magnetic resonance imaging showed a heterogeneous, expansile mass measuring 6 (anteroposterior) × 3.1 (transverse) × 5 (craniocaudal) cm within the right nasal cavity extending to the nasopharynx, with obliteration of the nasopharyngeal airway and anteroinferior displacement of the soft palate (Figure, B). The adjacent sinuses had drainage obstruction. Biopsy results showed fragments of necrotic and fibrinous debris with acute inflammatory exudate and bacterial colonies. Findings during surgery included a fibrous expansile mass filling the right nasal cavity and bowing the septum to the left. It crossed the midline to fill the nasopharynx and extended inferiorly toward the oropharynx. The mass was noted to originate at the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus. case_info.explanation: Of the 5 histological subtypes of sinonasal polyps (edematous, glandular, fibrous, cystic, and angiomatous or angiectatic), angiomatous nasal polyps (ANPs) make up about 4% to 5% of these sinonasal lesions.1Sinonasal polyps may present with nasal obstruction, facial pain or pressure, snoring, anosmia, epistaxis, and nasal drainage.2Some reports of ANPs describe a foul odor associated with the lesions, raising concern for bacterial, fungal, or malignant processes.3These presenting symptoms, however, are nonspecific, and additional workup must be completed to assess for other causes, such as inverted papilloma (IP), sinonasal tract angiofibroma (STA), and lobular capillary hemangioma (LCH). On computed tomography, ANPs typically present as a heterogenous density with minimal enhancement at the lesion’s edges and accompanying bony changes.4When visualized on magnetic resonance imaging, ANPs display heterogeneous isointense signal intensity on T1-weighted images and a hypointense peripheral rim on T2-weighted images.5IPs may have similar imaging appearance and display hypointense T1 signal with isointense or hypointense signal on T2-weighted image; contrast enhancement is in a convoluted cerebriform pattern.6Imaging of LCHs often show bone destruction and evidence of phleboliths.7STAs typically demonstrate heterogenous signal intensity on T1-weighted images and may be either high intensity or isointensity predominant on T2-weighted images.8Internal flow voids and intense enhancement are also seen in the majority of STAs, as well as LCHs.7In STAs, involvement of the sphenopalatine foramen/pterygopalatine fossa is often present,8which is not seen in ANPs. Location of origin is another factor that may differentiate these tumors. ANPs typically originate from the maxillary sinus and may spread to the choana.4LCHs most commonly originate from the anterior nasal septum, while STAs originate from the sphenopalatine foramen region along the posterior nasal cavity.7Alternatively, IPs usually arise from the lateral nasal wall or the paranasal sinuses. Imaging findings for this patient reflect ANP, with a large heterogeneous expansile mass extending from the right nasal cavity to the nasopharynx and into the posterior aspect of the maxillary sinus, with mass effect and mild resorption of the surrounding bones. When examined via light microscopy, ANPs often have an ulcerated roof and areas lined by respiratory epithelium, which may show squamous metaplasia.2ANPs also show scattered atypical pleomorphic spindle cells in the stroma, a paucity of inflammatory infiltrate, and abundant amorphous, Congo red–negative material.1ANPs are characterized by a high degree of vascular proliferation and ectasia; as such, these blood vessels may be subject to compression leading to infarction.3Given the highly vascularized and potentially necrotic nature of ANPs, it is understandable that these polyps may present with diagnostic difficulty due to potential confusion with other vascular tumors. Fully developed LCHs typically display lobules of back-to-back capillaries, with endothelial cells divided by fibrous or myxoid septa.9STAs, on the other hand, demonstrate a dense stromal component with numerous fibroblasts and have varying levels of vessel density. Immunohistochemical stains are also helpful in differentiating STAs from other tumors and will be positive for β-catenin, androgen receptor, estrogen receptor β, and prostate-specific antigen.7IPs are characterized histologically by an inverted appearance due to thickened epithelium enclosed by basement membrane, along with transmigrating intraepithelial neutrophilic inflammation.6The pathology and immunohistochemistry findings, as outlined in this case, align with ANP. The standard treatment for ANPs is resection via endoscopic approach. This treatment allows for symptom relief and a definitive pathologic characterization. Removal of the site of origin of these polyps is crucial for preventing recurrence. The present patient underwent successful endoscopic resection and followed up regularly outpatient after surgery. The patient’s presenting symptoms have resolved, and there was no evidence of recurrence at 6 months.

case_info.scenario: A 16-year-old male with a history of mild seasonal allergies presented with right-sided congestion, thick discolored nasal drainage, facial pain/pressure, anosmia, and intermittent epistaxis for approximately 1 year. Nasal endoscopy revealed moderate global deviation of the septum to the left. On the right, thick mucus and crusting anterior to the middle turbinate was seen, completely occluding the nasal cavity. Physical examination was otherwise normal. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a heterogeneous, expansile mass measuring 6 (anteroposterior) × 3.1 (transverse) × 5 (craniocaudal) cm within the right nasal cavity extending to the nasopharynx, with obliteration of the nasopharyngeal airway and anteroinferior displacement of the soft palate (Figure, B). The adjacent sinuses had drainage obstruction. Biopsy results showed fragments of necrotic and fibrinous debris with acute inflammatory exudate and bacterial colonies. Findings during surgery included a fibrous expansile mass filling the right nasal cavity and bowing the septum to the left. It crossed the midline to fill the nasopharynx and extended inferiorly toward the oropharynx. The mass was noted to originate at the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus. Pathologic evaluation showed fragments of polypoidal mucosa with edematous stroma, numerous ectatic vascular channels, and a sprinkling of inflammatory cells (Figure, A). The surface epithelium was largely ulcerated, covered with fibrinous and inflammatory debris and bacterial colonies. Immunostaining showed CD31 and CD34 positivity. Stromal cells did not have β-catenin present. Elastic stain results showed scant elastic fibers in the vascular proliferation.

case_info.explanation: Of the 5 histological subtypes of sinonasal polyps (edematous, glandular, fibrous, cystic, and angiomatous or angiectatic), angiomatous nasal polyps (ANPs) make up about 4% to 5% of these sinonasal lesions.1Sinonasal polyps may present with nasal obstruction, facial pain or pressure, snoring, anosmia, epistaxis, and nasal drainage.2Some reports of ANPs describe a foul odor associated with the lesions, raising concern for bacterial, fungal, or malignant processes.3These presenting symptoms, however, are nonspecific, and additional workup must be completed to assess for other causes, such as inverted papilloma (IP), sinonasal tract angiofibroma (STA), and lobular capillary hemangioma (LCH). On computed tomography, ANPs typically present as a heterogenous density with minimal enhancement at the lesion’s edges and accompanying bony changes.4When visualized on magnetic resonance imaging, ANPs display heterogeneous isointense signal intensity on T1-weighted images and a hypointense peripheral rim on T2-weighted images.5IPs may have similar imaging appearance and display hypointense T1 signal with isointense or hypointense signal on T2-weighted image; contrast enhancement is in a convoluted cerebriform pattern.6Imaging of LCHs often show bone destruction and evidence of phleboliths.7STAs typically demonstrate heterogenous signal intensity on T1-weighted images and may be either high intensity or isointensity predominant on T2-weighted images.8Internal flow voids and intense enhancement are also seen in the majority of STAs, as well as LCHs.7In STAs, involvement of the sphenopalatine foramen/pterygopalatine fossa is often present,8which is not seen in ANPs. Location of origin is another factor that may differentiate these tumors. ANPs typically originate from the maxillary sinus and may spread to the choana.4LCHs most commonly originate from the anterior nasal septum, while STAs originate from the sphenopalatine foramen region along the posterior nasal cavity.7Alternatively, IPs usually arise from the lateral nasal wall or the paranasal sinuses. Imaging findings for this patient reflect ANP, with a large heterogeneous expansile mass extending from the right nasal cavity to the nasopharynx and into the posterior aspect of the maxillary sinus, with mass effect and mild resorption of the surrounding bones. When examined via light microscopy, ANPs often have an ulcerated roof and areas lined by respiratory epithelium, which may show squamous metaplasia.2ANPs also show scattered atypical pleomorphic spindle cells in the stroma, a paucity of inflammatory infiltrate, and abundant amorphous, Congo red–negative material.1ANPs are characterized by a high degree of vascular proliferation and ectasia; as such, these blood vessels may be subject to compression leading to infarction.3Given the highly vascularized and potentially necrotic nature of ANPs, it is understandable that these polyps may present with diagnostic difficulty due to potential confusion with other vascular tumors. Fully developed LCHs typically display lobules of back-to-back capillaries, with endothelial cells divided by fibrous or myxoid septa.9STAs, on the other hand, demonstrate a dense stromal component with numerous fibroblasts and have varying levels of vessel density. Immunohistochemical stains are also helpful in differentiating STAs from other tumors and will be positive for β-catenin, androgen receptor, estrogen receptor β, and prostate-specific antigen.7IPs are characterized histologically by an inverted appearance due to thickened epithelium enclosed by basement membrane, along with transmigrating intraepithelial neutrophilic inflammation.6The pathology and immunohistochemistry findings, as outlined in this case, align with ANP. The standard treatment for ANPs is resection via endoscopic approach. This treatment allows for symptom relief and a definitive pathologic characterization. Removal of the site of origin of these polyps is crucial for preventing recurrence. The present patient underwent successful endoscopic resection and followed up regularly outpatient after surgery. The patient’s presenting symptoms have resolved, and there was no evidence of recurrence at 6 months.
